hints: Think about what makes the d block special, focus on the d orbitals in the element itself or in one of its stable ions, not just the electron configuration of the atom.
walkthrough:
Pin down the key test**
Many d block elements look like transition elements, but the real test is not the atom. Look at the ions it forms. Cobalt itself is $\text{[Ar]}3\text{d}^74\text{s}^2$, but what matters is $\text{Co}^{2+}$ is $3\text{d}^7$ and $\text{Co}^{3+}$ is $3\text{d}^6$. Both have an incomplete d set, so cobalt passes the test.
Final answer: An element that forms one or more stable ions with partially filled d orbitals.

hints: Recall the three classic reaction types for $[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$: $\text{OH}^-$ gives a hydroxide precipitate, excess $\text{Cl}^-$ gives a tetrahedral chloro complex, excess $\text{NH}_3$ gives an ammine complex by ligand exchange.

Check charges and coordination numbers: hydroxide precipitate is neutral $\text{Co}(\text{OH})_2$, chloro complex is $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$, ammine complex is $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{2+}$ (oxidised in air to 3+).
walkthrough:
Sort precipitation from substitution**
With $\text{OH}^-(\text{aq})$, water ligands are not simply swapped. Hydroxide removes $\text{H}^+$ and precipitates the neutral hydroxide. So A is $\text{Co}(\text{OH})_2$, you can also write it as $\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4(\text{OH})_2$.

Spot the tetrahedral chloro complex**
Excess concentrated $\text{Cl}^-$ replaces all six waters to give a tetrahedral complex with coordination number 4. Cobalt stays +2, four $\text{Cl}^-$ give overall 2-, so B is $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$.

Spot the ammine complex**
Excess $\text{NH}_3(\text{aq})$ acts as a ligand and exchanges for water to give an octahedral hexaammine. So C is $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{2+}$, which is readily oxidised by air to $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$. Either is accepted.

Final answer: A = $\text{Co}(\text{OH})_2$ or $\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4(\text{OH})_2$
B = $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$
C = $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{2+}$ or $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$

hints: Picture the starting solution of $[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ in a test tube and recall its characteristic pale colour.
Link ligand change to colour change: chloro substitution to $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$ gives an intense blue, ammine substitution gives a brown or yellow solution.
walkthrough:
Learn the colour fingerprints**
Colour is a direct fingerprint of ligand and geometry. Hexaaquacobalt(II) is pink. When $\text{Cl}^-$ forms tetrahedral $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$ the d splitting changes completely and the solution turns an intense blue.

Remember the ammine colour**
Replacing water by $\text{NH}_3$ to give the hexaammine changes the ligand field again. The solution becomes brown, yellow or orange depending on oxidation to Co(III). Any one of those colours is correct.
Final answer: $[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ pink; solution of B blue; solution of C brown / yellow / orange.

hints: Think of electrode potential as a comparison: the voltage of your half cell measured against a reference half cell, the standard hydrogen electrode.
Recall the three standard conditions that must be stated: ion concentration $1 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$, gas pressure 1 atm, temperature 298 K.
walkthrough:
Understand comparison to hydrogen**
You can never measure an absolute half cell potential. You always connect it to the standard hydrogen electrode, $\text{Pt} | \text{H}_2 | \text{H}^+$, and the voltage you read is the standard electrode potential of your electrode.

Add the standard conditions**
For the value to be standard, everything must be in standard states. That means all ions at $1 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$, any gas at 1 atm (101 kPa) and a temperature of 298 K. Quote these to earn the second mark.

Final answer: The emf of a half cell compared to / connected to a standard hydrogen electrode
with solutions of concentration $1 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$, gases at 1 atm pressure and 298 K.

hints: Decide if each half cell contains a metal: $\text{Co}^{2+}$/Co has solid Co available, while $\text{Fe}^{3+}$/$\text{Fe}^{2+}$ has only ions so needs an inert conductor.
walkthrough:
Choose active versus inert**
For $\text{Co}^{2+}$/Co, cobalt metal itself conducts and takes part, so use a Co rod. For $\text{Fe}^{3+}$/$\text{Fe}^{2+}$ both species are in solution, so you need an inert surface to carry electrons without reacting. Platinum, carbon or graphite all work.
Final answer: $\text{Co}^{2+}$/Co electrode: Co (cobalt metal); $\text{Fe}^{3+}$/$\text{Fe}^{2+}$ electrode: Pt or carbon / graphite.

hints: Use $E^{\circ}$ values: $\text{Fe}^{3+}$/$\text{Fe}^{2+}$ (+0.77 V) is more positive than $\text{Co}^{2+}$/Co (-0.28 V), so Fe(III) is reduced and Co is oxidised; balance electrons 2 to 1.
walkthrough:
Combine the half equations correctly**
The more positive electrode gains electrons. So $\text{Fe}^{3+} + e^- \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{2+}$ happens twice, while $\text{Co} \rightarrow \text{Co}^{2+} + 2e^-$. Add them and cancel the $2e^-$ to give $\text{Co} + 2\text{Fe}^{3+} \rightarrow \text{Co}^{2+} + 2\text{Fe}^{2+}$.

hints: Apply $E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{positive}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{negative}} = (+0.77) - (-0.28)$ from the Data Booklet.
walkthrough:
Subtract the right way**
Take the reduction potential of the positive Fe half cell minus that of the negative Co half cell: $$E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}} = 0.77 - (-0.28) = +1.05 \text{ V}$$ Double minus gives plus, so the cell is strongly feasible.
Final answer: $E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = 0.77 - (-0.28) = +1.05 \text{ V}$

hints: Substitute into $E = E^{\circ} + (0.059/z)\log[\text{Co}^{2+}]$ with $E^{\circ} = -0.28 \text{ V}$, $z = 2$ and $[\text{Co}^{2+}] = 0.050$.
walkthrough:
Plug into Nernst carefully**
For $\text{Co}^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{Co}$, $z = 2$. Lower ion concentration shifts equilibrium toward ions, making $E$ more negative: $$E = -0.28 + \frac{0.059}{2}\log(0.050)$$ $$E = -0.28 + 0.0295 \times (-1.30) = -0.28 - 0.038 = -0.32 \text{ V}$$

hints: Think how $E_{\text{cell}} = E_{\text{Fe}} - E_{\text{Co}}$ changes when $E_{\text{Co}}$ becomes more negative while $E_{\text{Fe}}$ stays standard.
walkthrough:
Track the subtraction**
$E_{\text{cell}} = E_{\text{Fe}} - E_{\text{Co}}$. You just made $E_{\text{Co}}$ more negative, from -0.28 to -0.32 V. Subtracting a more negative number gives a larger result, so $E_{\text{cell}}$ becomes more positive than $E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}}$.

hints: With excess $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ as oxidant, vanadium(0) is oxidised to its highest stable oxidation state in acid, $\text{V}(+4)$ as $\text{VO}^{2+}$; check Data Booklet $E^{\circ}$ values to confirm feasibility.
Balance V to Fe as 1 to 4 for electron change ($\text{V} \rightarrow \text{V(IV)} + 4e^-$), then balance O with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and H with $\text{H}^+$.
walkthrough:
Pick the final vanadium species**
Excess $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ drives vanadium as far as it can go. In acid the $\text{V(IV)}$ oxocation $\text{VO}^{2+}$ is the product, not $\text{V}^{2+}$ or $\text{V}^{3+}$. Vanadium goes from 0 to +4, losing 4 electrons.

Balance the redox equation**
Each $\text{Fe}^{3+} + e^- \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{2+}$ takes 1 electron, so you need 4 $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ per V: $$\text{V} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{VO}^{2+} + 2\text{H}^+ + 4e^-$$ Add $4\text{Fe}^{3+} + 4e^- \rightarrow 4\text{Fe}^{2+}$ and cancel electrons to give: $$4\text{Fe}^{3+} + \text{V} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{VO}^{2+} + 4\text{Fe}^{2+} + 2\text{H}^+$$ Check atoms and charge: 12+ both sides, 1 V, 4 Fe, 1 O, 2 H.

Final answer: Product: $\text{VO}^{2+}$
$4\text{Fe}^{3+} + \text{V} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{VO}^{2+} + 4\text{Fe}^{2+} + 2\text{H}^+$
